title: Latent labour, early assessment and prelabour rupture of membranes
blurb: Triage and support women in latent labour, and manage prelabour rupture of membranes at term under NICE NG235.
question: Lauren, 39+2 weeks, phones the birth centre. She had a gush of clear fluid 2 hours ago and has no contractions. She is well, her baby is moving normally and she has no risk factors, including no group B streptococcus. What should the midwife advise?

teach.body: Formally: the latent first stage is a period, not necessarily continuous, of contractions with some cervical change up to 4 cm. Prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) at term is rupture of the membranes at or after 37+0 weeks before labour begins. In plain English: early labour can stop and start and is often best spent at home with good support; waters breaking before labour is common, and most women go into labour within a day.

teach.h: A woman calls in early labour

steps.label: Early assessment
steps.sub: at home or planned place of birth; 1:1 for at least 1 hour

steps.label: Not established?
steps.sub: individual support and analgesia if needed

steps.label: Home or stay
steps.sub: encourage home unless risk of unattended birth or distress

teach.caption: NICE NG235 1.8.2–1.8.6. The triage midwife documents the guidance she gives.

teach.h: Every early or triage assessment includes
items: Ask how she is, her wishes, expectations and concerns.
Ask about the baby's movements, including any change.
Explain what to expect in latent labour and how to work with the pain.
Explain what to expect when she accesses care.
Agree a plan, including who to contact next and when.
Guide and support her birth companion(s).

teach.h: Suspected PROM: attend now if any of these
head: Risk factor on phone triage
Why
rows: Vaginal bleeding or continuous abdominal pain
GBS carriage with a plan for antibiotics
Abnormal lie, FGR or low-lying placenta
teach.caption: NICE NG235 1.7.1. Any uncertainty also means attending for urgent in-person review.

root.label: Waters broken, 37+0 or more, no labour

children.edge: GBS positive this pregnancy, or previous baby with GBS
children.label: Offer immediate induction

teach.caption: NICE NG235 1.7.2, 1.7.6, 1.7.11. If labour has not started after about 24 hours, offer induction.

items.label: risk of serious neonatal infection (0.5% with intact membranes)
offer induction if labour has not started
minimum stay after birth if ROM over 24 h

teach.body: Do not do a speculum if rupture is certain; if uncertain, offer a speculum and avoid digital vaginal examination without contractions. While waiting: she records her temperature every 4 hours while awake and reports any change in colour or smell of her loss at once. Bathing or showering does not increase infection, but sex may. Do not offer lower vaginal swabs or CRP. Assess fetal movements and heart rate at first contact and every 24 hours.

Lauren has no risk factors, so the midwife arranges to see her in person within 12 hours (sooner if she has concerns or wants induction now), at home, in the midwifery unit or an assessment centre. At review she explains the 1% infection risk, that 60% labour within 24 hours, and the choice of waiting up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible. Lauren chooses to wait, with clear advice on temperature, loss and movements.

teach.text: No digital vaginal examination with PROM and no contractions, and no speculum when rupture is certain. If labour has not started 24 hours after rupture, she should give birth where there is access to neonatal services and stay at least 12 hours.

items: Latent labour: cervical change up to 4 cm; support at home where safe.
Early assessment at home or planned place of birth, one-to-one for at least 1 hour.
Term PROM: phone triage; attend now if risk factors; otherwise see within 12 hours.
Choice of expectant management up to 24 h or induction as soon as possible.
GBS positive: immediate induction (or planned caesarean).
After ROM over 24 h: neonatal services, 12-hour stay, baby observed at 1, 2, 6, 12 h.

summary: You can now triage and support women in latent labour and assess them early at home or their planned place of birth. You can also manage prelabour rupture of membranes at term, including risk factors needing attendance, the 24-hour choice, the GBS pathway and care of the baby afterwards.

A.q: Abi, 39 weeks, is unsure whether her waters have broken. She has no contractions. What should the midwife offer?
options: A digital vaginal examination
A lower vaginal swab for culture
A speculum examination
A maternal CRP blood test
A.why: NG235 1.7.4: if it is uncertain whether PROM has occurred, offer a speculum examination and avoid digital vaginal examination in the absence of contractions.

whyNot.0: Digital VE without contractions should be avoided because of infection risk.
whyNot.1: Lower vaginal swabs are not offered in PROM at term (NG235 1.7.8).
whyNot.3: CRP is not offered to detect infection after term PROM.

A.q: Hana has prelabour rupture of membranes at 38 weeks. What is the risk of serious neonatal infection that the midwife should explain?
options: About 1%, compared with 0.5% with intact membranes
About 5%, compared with 1% with intact membranes
About 0.1%, compared with 0.05% with intact membranes
About 10%, compared with 1% with intact membranes
A.why: NG235 1.7.5: the risk of serious neonatal infection is 1%, rather than 0.5% for women with intact membranes.

whyNot.1: This overstates the risk given in NG235.
whyNot.2: This understates the risk given in NG235.

A.q: Joy, 39+1 weeks, has PROM. A swab earlier in this pregnancy grew group B streptococcus. What should be offered?
options: Expectant management for up to 24 hours
Expectant management for up to 12 hours
Antibiotics and waiting for labour at home
Immediate induction of labour
A.why: NG235 1.7.11 and NG207 1.2.16: with term PROM and a positive GBS test in this pregnancy, offer immediate induction (or caesarean birth if already planned).

whyNot.0: Expectant management is for women without GBS carriage.
whyNot.1: A shorter wait is still not the recommended plan.
whyNot.2: Waiting at home is not recommended with known GBS and ruptured membranes.

B.q: Rosie, in her first labour, attends the midwifery unit with painful irregular contractions. She is 2 cm dilated and she and her baby are well. She lives 10 minutes away. What is the most appropriate care?
options: Admit her to the unit and start an oxytocin infusion
Support, analgesia if needed, and home if she agrees
Perform an amniotomy to help establish her labour
Admit her to the labour ward for continuous CTG
B.why: NG235 1.8.6: recognise painful contractions without established labour, give individualised support and analgesia if needed, and encourage her to remain at or return home unless there is a risk of unattended birth or distress.

whyNot.0: Oxytocin is not used to manage normal latent labour.
whyNot.2: Amniotomy is not used for latent labour.
whyNot.3: There is no indication for continuous CTG.

B.q: Sana chooses expectant management after term PROM. Which advice should the midwife give?
options: Avoid baths and showers until labour starts
Have a lower vaginal swab taken each day
Record her temperature 4-hourly while awake
Have a CRP blood test taken every 24 hours
B.why: NG235 1.7.8: advise recording temperature every 4 hours during waking hours and reporting any change in colour or smell of her vaginal loss.

whyNot.0: Bathing or showering is not associated with an increase in infection.
whyNot.1: Lower vaginal swabs are not offered.

B.q: Labour has not started 24 hours after Mai's membranes ruptured at term. Where should she be advised to give birth, and for how long should she stay afterwards?
options: Where neonatal services are available; stay at least 12 hours
A freestanding midwifery unit; discharge home 6 hours after birth
Obstetric unit; stay at least 48 hours after the birth
Any setting she prefers; baby observed for the first 2 hours
B.why: NG235 1.7.10: give birth where there is access to neonatal services (obstetric unit or alongside midwifery unit) and stay in hospital for at least 12 hours after the birth.

whyNot.1: A freestanding unit lacks on-site neonatal services, and 6 hours is too short.
whyNot.2: 48 hours is longer than NG235 requires.
whyNot.3: Birth should be where neonatal services are available, and observations extend to 12 hours.

C.q: Mira, 38+4 weeks, phones to say her waters broke an hour ago and the fluid is green-tinged. She has no contractions. What should the midwife advise?
options: A home review within the next 12 hours
Expectant management for up to 24 hours
Ring back when contractions start
Attend the unit now for urgent review
C.why: NG235 1.7.1: meconium-stained liquor is a risk factor on phone triage; she should attend immediately for an urgent in-person review.

whyNot.0: A 12-hour review is for women without risk factors.
whyNot.1: Expectant management is not appropriate before urgent assessment of meconium.
whyNot.2: Waiting for contractions delays assessment of possible fetal compromise.

C.q: Tia, 39+5 weeks, phones with suspected PROM. She has no risk factors on triage and no concerns. When should she be seen in person?
options: At the 24-hour point if not in labour
Within 12 hours, or sooner if she wishes
When contractions become regular
Within 72 hours at the antenatal clinic
C.why: NG235 1.7.2: with no risk factors, see her in person as soon as possible if she has concerns or wants induction, or within 12 hours, at home, a midwifery unit or an assessment centre.

whyNot.0: Waiting 24 hours misses the review needed to offer her choices.
whyNot.2: Review is planned, not left until labour.
whyNot.3: 72 hours is far beyond the recommended time frame.

C.q: Lily's baby is born well. Her membranes ruptured 30 hours before she was in established labour, and the baby shows no signs of infection. What care does the baby need?
options: IV antibiotics started within 1 hour
Observations at 1 and 2 hours, then discharge
Observations at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours
A temperature check before discharge
C.why: NG235 1.11.31–1.11.32: if membranes ruptured more than 24 hours before established labour, observe the baby at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours; do not give antibiotics without signs of infection.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics are not given to a well baby with no signs of infection.
whyNot.3: A single check is not enough after prolonged rupture.

reteach.title: Phone, see, choose
reteach.question: When a woman rings to say her waters have gone, think in three steps. What happens at each?

blocks.body: Phone: when did they break, and are there risk factors (meconium, blood, reduced movements, pain, smell, feeling unwell, GBS, abnormal lie, FGR, low-lying placenta)? Any yes means come in now. See: otherwise review in person within 12 hours. Choose: wait up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible, unless GBS positive, when immediate induction is offered.

blocks.text: Speculum only when unsure; no fingers without contractions.

explain.body: After telephone triage, a face-to-face early assessment can be at home (whatever the planned place of birth) or in her planned place of birth, with one-to-one midwifery care for at least 1 hour.

test.q: Where can a face-to-face early assessment of labour take place under NICE NG235?
options: At home or her planned place of birth
In the obstetric unit for every woman
By telephone, with no visit required
At her GP surgery the following day
test.why: NG235 1.8.3: at home (regardless of planned place of birth) or in her planned place of birth, with one-to-one care for at least 1 hour.

whyNot.1: Women planning midwifery-led or home birth do not need to attend an obstetric unit.
whyNot.2: Telephone triage decides whether face-to-face assessment is needed; it does not replace it.
whyNot.3: A GP surgery is not a setting for labour assessment.

explain.body: Ask when the waters broke and check for risk factors. If any is present, or there is uncertainty, she attends immediately for urgent review.

test.q: Which finding on phone triage after suspected term PROM means the woman should attend straight away?
options: Clear, odourless liquor
Waters broke 2 hours ago
Mild backache in the evening
Reduced fetal movements
test.why: NG235 1.7.1 lists reduced fetal movements as a risk factor requiring immediate attendance.

whyNot.1: Timing alone is not a risk factor at 2 hours.
whyNot.2: Mild backache is not a listed risk factor.

explain.body: Assess fetal movements and heart rate at the first contact and then every 24 hours after rupture while she is not in labour, and advise her to report any decrease in movements at once.

test.q: During expectant management after term PROM, how often should fetal movements and heart rate be assessed?
options: Every 4 hours using a CTG
At first contact, then every 24 hours
Every 12 hours by intermittent auscultation
From the time that labour starts
test.why: NG235 1.7.9: assess fetal movement and heart rate at initial contact and then every 24 hours while she is not in labour.

whyNot.3: Assessment starts at first contact, not at labour.

explain.body: 60% of women with term PROM go into labour within 24 hours. If labour has not started after about 24 hours, offer induction. Respect a choice to wait longer and discuss her options.

test.q: What proportion of women with term PROM go into labour within 24 hours?
options: About 20%
About 95%
About 60%
About 40%
test.why: NG235 1.7.5: 60% of women with prelabour rupture of membranes will go into labour within 24 hours.

whyNot.3: 40% is the proportion not yet in labour by 24 hours.
